summary: This is a LANGUAGE topic: the vocabulary of data handling — data, tally, tally chart, frequency, frequency table, survey, pictogram, bar chart, axis/axes, scale, label, category, discrete data, continuous data, line graph, pie chart. The words are learned by USING them while collecting, organising and presenting real data, not by reciting definitions. Two load-bearing distinctions carry the topic: frequency (the COUNT) versus tally (the marks) versus category (the group); and discrete (separate values, usually counted, often whole numbers) versus continuous (measured, can take values in between). Introduce each term at the moment it is needed in a real data activity, and lean on contrast pairs, because the meaning of 'continuous' lives in its contrast with 'discrete'.
misconceptions: Confuses discrete and continuous — e.g. thinks height is discrete because it's written as a whole number, or that 'continuous' just means 'a lot of data'
Uses 'frequency' for the category name, or conflates the tally marks with the frequency total
Muddles 'label' and 'scale' — calls the category names the scale, or numbers an axis in uneven steps yet still calls it a scale
Calls every display a 'bar chart' or 'graph', not matching the term to the representation

activities.title: Label the chart and sort the data
steps: Finish a half-built bar chart by placing the right term onto each part: the title, each axis label, the scale (the equal number steps up the side), the category names along the bottom, and the frequency (the count shown by the height of each bar on the value axis).
Say each term aloud as you place it — 'this is the scale', 'these are the category names', 'this axis shows the frequency' — so you are wielding the word, not just matching it.
Sort real variables into 'discrete (counted)' or 'continuous (measured)': e.g. 'number of pets', 'goals scored' versus 'how tall', 'time taken', 'temperature'.
For each variable, apply the test: 'Could there be a value in between?' — someone can be 125-and-a-half cm tall (continuous) but cannot have two-and-a-half pets (discrete).
activities.insight: Data vocabulary is mastered by using it correctly in a real chart and a real sorting task — height is continuous because a value can fall in between, even when it is written as a whole number.

activities.title: Tally to frequency: marks become a count
steps: Run a quick survey (e.g. favourite fruit) and record responses by making tally marks in a tally chart as each one comes in.

When counting is done, total each row and write the frequency in a frequency table — pointing out that the tally is the marks and the frequency is the final count. Then show the same frequencies as a pictogram, with a key that says what one picture stands for, and say 'this is a pictogram' while you build it.
As you work, answer: 'Which part is the tally and which is the frequency?' and 'Which part is the category?'
activities.insight: Tally (the marks), frequency (the count) and category (the group) are three different roles; the tally feeds the frequency, they are not the same thing.

activities.title: Contrast-pair glossary (scaffold)
steps: View 'discrete' and 'continuous' side by side, each with a canonical example and the 'could there be a value in between?' test.
View 'tally' beside 'frequency', and 'label' beside 'scale', comparing what each one does.
Tap or point to parts of a chart to reveal their names, then try to name the next part before revealing it.
activities.insight: Tricky terms are easier to hold when seen as contrast pairs, because the meaning sits in the difference between the two words.

checkQuestion: We counted how many pets each child has, and we also measured how tall everyone is. Set up a bar chart for the pet data and talk me through it as you go — and for each of the two things we collected, tell me whether it's discrete or continuous. (Listen for the terms USED correctly in the activity, not for definitions.)
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for correct USE in context: naming the title, axis labels, an even scale and the categories; using 'frequency' for the counts and 'tally' for the marks; and identifying number of pets as discrete (counted, whole) and height as continuous (measured, can fall between values), justified by the 'in-between' test.
